headline: Take, “bamboo”, has several derivation theories, one linking it to words for height: 高 (taka), 長 (take), 丈 (take).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *takai.
Theories on derivation include:
* From 長(たけ)生(おう) (takeou) or 高(たか)生(はえ) (takahae), in reference to the speed at which bamboo grows.
* Cognate with 高(たか) (taka), 長(たけ) (take), 丈(たけ) (take), all “height”.
* From 高(たか)景(かけ) (takakake) or つらこえ (tsurakoe).
* From ta meaning “tall” (高(たか)い (takai)) + ke, ancient combining form of 木(き) (ki, “tree”).
* A contraction of 痛(いた)快(く)茎(き)延(は)へ (itakukihae), referring to the speed at which bamboo grows.
* From ta, from Korean 대 (dae, “bamboo”) (see also 대나무 (daenamu, “bamboo”, literally “bamboo tree”)), + ke, ancient combining form of 木(き) (ki).

meaning: Take care of yourself, Take care!, Get well soon
headline: Odaiji ni is お (o) plus 大事 (daiji, “important”) plus に (ni), shortened from お大事になさってください (o daiji ni nasatte kudasai).

sources.quote: From お (o, honorific marker) + 大(だい)事(じ) (daiji, “important”) + に (ni, particle for direction); shortened from expressions such as お大(だい)事(じ)になさってください (o daiji ni nasatte kudasai, “Please take care of yourself”).

examples.ja: どうぞお大事に。
examples.en: Please take care of yourself.

examples.ja: お体をお大事に。
examples.en: Take care of yourself.

headline: Ageru is from Old Japanese 上ぐ (agu), from Proto-Japonic *ank-a-.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 上ぐ (agu), following 下二段活用 (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”), from Proto-Japonic *ank-a-.
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

headline: Ueru is from the classical verb 植う (uu).

sources.quote: */uwu/ → /uweru/ → /ueru/
From classical verb 植う (uu).
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

examples.ja: 私は庭にバラを植えた。
examples.en: I planted roses in the garden.

examples.ja: 彼女は庭に木犀を植えた。
examples.en: She planted fragrant olives in the garden.

headline: Fukuro is very likely related to 含む (fukumu, “to include”) and 膨れる (fukureru, “to swell”), from a root *puk-.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. From Proto-Japonic *pukoro.
Very likely related to 含む (fukumu, “to include”), also among others deriving from a root *puk- (e.g. 膨れる (fukureru, “to swell”)).

examples.ja: 犯人は袋の中の鼠だ。
examples.en: The culprit is caught like a rat in a trap.

examples.ja: 男は袋を肩に担いだ。
examples.en: The man threw a bag across his shoulder.

meaning: Mister (mostly in addressing someone on an envelope)

sources.quote: The tono changes to dono as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: Mugen may be a learned borrowing from Chinese 無限 (wúxiàn, literally “without + limit”), first cited to 1881 as a translation of English infinite.

sources.quote: May be a learned borrowing from Chinese 無限 /无限 (wúxiàn, literally “without + limit”). First cited to 1881 in the 哲学字彙 (Tetsugaku Jii, “Philosophical Vocabulary”) as a translation of English infinite.

examples.ja: 石油の供給は無限ではない。
examples.en: Supplies of oil are not infinite.

examples.ja: 宇宙は無限に膨張し続けるのか？
examples.en: Will the universe expand indefinitely?

headline: Tenrankai is 展覧 (tenran, “exhibition”) plus 会 (-kai, “gathering”).

sources.quote: 展覧(てんらん) (tenran, “exhibition”) + 会(かい) (-kai, “gathering”)

examples.en: Did you go to the art exhibition?

examples.en: We hold an exhibition every year.

headline: Tera appears in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE; some sources derive it from an ancestor of Middle Korean 졀 (jeol), likely Baekje.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Appears in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE, and in the Man'yōshū, completed some time after 759 CE.
There are various theories regarding the ultimate derivation.

* Some sources derive Japanese tera from an ancestor of Middle Korean 졀 (jeol) (likely Baekje). This is from earlier 뎔 (dyeol, “temple”) and is the nativised reading of 찰 (刹, chal, “Buddhist temple”) below, deriving in turn from Middle Chinese 剎 (MC tsrhaet), shortened from 剎多羅 (MC tsrhaet ta la, “Buddhist monastery, temple or shrine”), borrowed from Sanskrit क्षेत्र (kṣetra, “land, area, domain”), from Proto-Indo-Aryan *ṭṣáytram, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *ćšáytram, from Proto-Indo-European *tḱéytrom.

* Other sources describe Japanese tera as cognate with modern Korean 찰 (刹, chal, “temple”), appearing as a component in terms such as 선찰 (禪刹, seonchal, “Zen temple”), 사찰 (寺刹, sachal, “Buddhist temple”).
* Another derivation is given as Pali thera (“elders”) in reference to the monks.

Considering the phonetic development in Korean, the avenues for transmission of Buddhist terms to Japan, and the consistent temple sense of the Japanese term throughout recorded history, the now-obsolete Korean 뎔 (dyeol, “temple”) may be a more likely source than Pali thera (“elders”).

examples.ja: 寺の隣に鬼が住む。
examples.en: The devil lurks behind the cross.

examples.ja: その寺にも行ったよ。
examples.en: We also went to the temple.

headline: Kago appears to be an uncertain element ka plus 籠 (ko), with ko voiced to go.

sources.quote: Appears to be derived from a compound of an uncertain element ka and 籠 (ko) below, with ko changing to go as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

examples.ja: 少年はかごから鳥を放した。

examples.ja: かごは苺でいっぱいでした。
examples.en: The basket was filled with strawberries.

meaning: to be happy; to be glad
headline: Ureshii might come from 熟れる (ureru, “to ripen, mature”) plus しい, though it is unclear how “feeling mature” matches “glad”.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. First cited to the Man'yōshu of circa 759 CE.

A surface analysis suggests that this might be derived from 熟れる (ureru, “to ripen, mature”) + しい (shii, “adjective forming suffix”). However, it is unclear how the sense of "feeling mature" would match the sense of "glad".

examples.ja: ああ嬉しい。
examples.en: How glad I am!

examples.ja: うれしくないの？
examples.en: Aren't you happy?

headline: Sukizuki is a reduplication of 好き (suki, “fondness”).

sources.quote: Reduplication of 好き (suki, “fondness”).

examples.ja: 音楽の好みは人によって好きずきです。

sources.quote: Compound of 昼(ひる) (hiru, “daytime; noon”) + 間(ま) (ma, “space; period”).

headline: Tsui, “pair”, is from Middle Chinese 對 (MC twojH).

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 對 (MC twojH).

examples.ja: この国の王は人ではなく、はるか天空に居られるという三対の翼を持つ神獣なんだ。

headline: Shiro's derivation is unknown; the reading first appears in 794 CE when 山背 (Yamashiro) was renamed 山城 by Emperor Kanmu.

sources.quote: Derivation unknown. The shiro reading for this character appears in 794 CE when the 山背 (Yamashiro) region was renamed 山城, by Emperor Kanmu, thus applying the shiro reading to the 城 kanji for the first time.

examples.ja: あの城は美しい。
examples.en: That castle is beautiful.

examples.ja: 遠方に城が見えた。

meaning: to turn back, to go back, reverse

sources.quote: 引(ひ)く (hiku, “to pull”) + 返(かえ)す (kaesu, “to return; to repeat”)

examples.en: He turned back halfway.

headline: Boro is described as shortened from ぼろぼろ (boroboro), first attested in 1736, though a homophone for beggar monks, 梵論, dates from the early 1300s.

sources.quote: Japanese sources describe this as a derivation via shortening from adjective and adverb ぼろぼろ (boroboro, “dilapidated, crumbling; dilapidatedly, crumblingly”), and give a first attestation of 1736.

However, there is a homophone spelled in kanji as 梵論 or 暮露, referring to poor mendicant beggar monks, first attested variously as boro or boron starting from the early 1300s, known also as 梵論字 (boronji) and reduplicated 梵論梵論 (boroboro). This type of monk evolved into the modern 虚無僧 (komusō, “monk of emptiness”) practice, while their older name may have given rise to the cluster of related terms with meanings surrounding senses of "dilapidated, worn-out, crumbling".
May be ultimately related to, or otherwise influenced by, verbs 滅びる (horobiru, “to fall to ruin, to crumble, to be destroyed”), 滅ぼす (horobosu, “to ruin, to make something crumble, to destroy”).

headline: Tsuya is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *tuya.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *tuya.

headline: Koi went from kopi through kofi and kowi to koi, from the stem of 恋う (kou, “to love, yearn”).

sources.quote: ⟨ko₁pi₂⟩ → /kʷopʷɨ/ → /kofi/ → /kowi/ → /koi/
From Old Japanese.
From the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 恋(こ)う (kou, “to love, yearn”).

examples.ja: 恋の味は苦い。

sources.quote: 通(とお)る (tōru, “to pass through”) + 掛(か)かる (kakaru)

sources.quote: Doublet of 移(うつ)る (utsuru, “to move; to transfer”).

examples.ja: うまく写っているといいですが。

headline: Shinkei was first used in the Kaitai Shinsho of 1774 by Sugita Genpaku and others, translating the Dutch zenuw.

sources.quote: The word 神(しん)経(けい) (shinkei) was first used in a book called Kaitai Shinsho (解体新書) published in Japan in 1774 by Sugita Genpaku (杉田玄白) and others as a translation of "Ontleedkundige Tafelen", the Dutch version of the original German book called "Anatomische Tabellen."

In order to translate the Dutch term "zenuw", Genpaku coined the word 神(しん)経(けい) (shinkei) by combining the word 神(しん)気(き) (shinki, “life energy”) and 経(けい)脈(みゃく) (keimyaku, “network of paths”). The original German medical book was published in 1734, and Genpaku and his colleagues spent three years translating the Dutch version and it is recognized as the first Japanese publication relating to the human anatomy as understood by the western medical science. The Dutch version was used because that was perhaps the only foreign language familiar to Japanese at that time as Dutch shipping was the only authorized merchant ships to enter Nagasaki, the only open port recognized by the Tokugawa Shogunate while Japan refused to deal with outside world under the strict isolation policy in effect at that time.

examples.ja: 神経は抜くのですか。
examples.en: Are you going to remove the nerve?

examples.ja: 神経を抜く必要があります。
examples.en: I have to remove your nerve.

headline: Tatakai is the continuative stem of 戦う (tatakau, “to fight”).

sources.quote: The 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 戦(たたか)う (tatakau, “to fight”).

examples.ja: 戦いに勝つ。
examples.en: We will win the day.

examples.ja: 戦いは終わった。
examples.en: The fight is over.

meaning: to lose (a game) (v.i.), to be defeated
headline: Makeru is from Old Japanese 負く (maku), from Proto-Japonic *mak-a-.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 負く (maku), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern, from Proto-Japonic *mak-a-.
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.
First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.

examples.ja: 負けるが勝ち。
examples.en: When you lose, you actually win.

examples.ja: 弱者は負ける。
examples.en: Weak people lose.

meaning: to be prolonged, to drag on
headline: Nagabiku is 長い (nagai) plus 引く (hiku).

sources.quote: 長(なが)い (nagai) + 引(ひ)く (hiku)

examples.ja: 長びきそうですか。
examples.en: Will it take long to recover?

examples.ja: その経済学者は長引く不況を予期していた。
examples.en: The economist anticipated a prolonged depression.

headline: Bō, “pole”, is from Middle Chinese 棒, the goon pronunciation, so likely an earlier borrowing.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 棒 (MC baewngX). The goon pronunciation, so likely an earlier borrowing.

examples.ja: 足が棒になった。
examples.en: My legs feel heavy as lead.

examples.ja: 彼は犬を棒でたたいた。
examples.en: He beat the dog with a stick.

headline: Gurasu is English glass, a doublet of ガラス (garasu), from Dutch.

sources.quote: Borrowed from English glass. Doublet of ガラス (garasu), from Dutch.

examples.ja: グラスは粉々に割れてしまった。
examples.en: The glass shattered into pieces.

headline: Katsuryoku is 活 (katsu, “life”) plus 力 (-ryoku, “power”).

sources.quote: 活(かつ) (katsu, “life”) + 力(りょく) (-ryoku, “power”)

examples.ja: 彼はいつも活力旺盛だ。

examples.ja: 彼は活力に満ち溢れている。
examples.en: He is full of energy.
